cf.title: Report oldest xmin source when autovacuum cannot remove tuples

input.subject: Report oldest xmin source when autovacuum cannot remove tuples

verdict_reasoning: No objection survived at level 1: the problem is stated, several independent people ask for it, and the cost falls only on instrumented vacuums. Two fixable design points remain at level 2. maintenance-fit-1 says GetXidHorizonBlocker() duplicates horizon rules and nothing fails when they drift from ComputeXidHorizons(). standards-compat-1 says the line names one holder where other diagnostic log lines list all. Both need a decision from someone who knows the ProcArray and slot horizon code.

brief.title: Report what held back the removable cutoff in VACUUM log output
brief.problem: When VACUUM leaves dead tuples behind, its log gives the removable cutoff but not what held it back. Users must check pg_stat_activity, pg_prepared_xacts and pg_replication_slots by hand, and by then the holder may be gone. This hurts DBAs who diagnose table bloat after the fact.
brief.proposed_design: v10 adds GetXidHorizonBlocker(), which scans the ProcArray and replication slots once, right after vacuum computes its cutoffs, and only for VACUUM (VERBOSE) or a logged autovacuum. It compares each proc's raw xid and raw xmin against the final horizon and reports the xid owner before a snapshot holder. VACUUM prints the result after the removable cutoff line when dead tuples were left unremovable.
user_visible_surface: New VACUUM (VERBOSE) and autovacuum log line: "removable cutoff was held back by: ...", for example "prepared transaction" or "transaction holding snapshot (pid = %d)".
The line names hot standby feedback only when the walsender holds the xmin without a slot, and names slots of any type by slot name.
New C function GetXidHorizonBlocker() in procarray.h, which extensions can call.
author_claims: Logs keep a durable record for analysis after the fact, which a view cannot give once the holder is gone.
A separate scan against the final horizon avoids the wrong-PID result that tracking inside ComputeXidHorizons() produced.
One extra shared ProcArrayLock scan per instrumented vacuum costs a few microseconds with 1000 backends.
The report is best-effort, so the line uses the past tense.
brief.thread_state: Many reviewers support the idea, and Japin Li, wenhui qiu and Laurenz Albe gave LGTM on v5. After Fujii Masao's offline comments, v10 narrowed the scope and moved to a single scan right after the cutoffs. Open points: wenhui qiu wants the active versus idle-in-transaction distinction back, Bharath's in-loop capture is still proposed, and nobody has reviewed v10 in the thread.
unclear: The full list of category strings and detail fields that v10 prints; only one example line and one quoted format are shown.
Whether v10 still reports the prepared transaction GID or standby application_name; message #53 calls the GID a follow-up.
How v10 breaks ties among snapshot holders at the same xmin, which Scott Ray said depends on scan order.
Whether v10 adds any documentation; the touched file list contains no doc files.
The end of message #51 is truncated, including part of the discussion about output surfaces.

objections.title: Second copy of horizon rules can drift from ComputeXidHorizons()
objections.failure_scenario: A later release adds a new horizon source, as retain_dead_tuples added pg_conflict_detection, and updates ComputeXidHorizons() and the slot code but not GetXidHorizonBlocker(). Nothing fails. VACUUM then prints no blocker or names the wrong one, and DBAs find out during a bloat incident.
objections.argument: GetXidHorizonBlocker() must match each proc's raw xid and xmin, slot effective_xmin and catalog_xmin, invalidation and per-database rules exactly as the horizon code does. Message #39 raised the drift risk, and message #42 shared only the per-database filter. Message #53 shows v9 already got one slot case wrong. The slot rules and any future sources stay duplicated, and no test fails when they diverge.
objections.author_must_show: Which horizon inputs does v10 share with ComputeXidHorizons() and the slot code, and what fails when a future horizon source is not added to GetXidHorizonBlocker()?

critic.reasoning: The thread shows a shared helper only for the per-database filter in v8, and the slot rules stay duplicated. The cost is a missing or wrong log line in a best-effort report, so it is fixable, but nothing fails loudly on drift.

objections.title: One reported blocker hides other holders at the same cutoff
objections.failure_scenario: A prepared transaction and a physical slot both hold the removable cutoff. VACUUM names only the prepared transaction, and the DBA commits it. The next vacuum, perhaps hours later on a large table, still leaves dead tuples behind and only then names the slot.
objections.argument: Message #52 points out that log_lock_waits, log_recovery_conflict_waits and deadlock reports list every holder, while v10 reduces the set to one entry. In message #17 the author answers that the next VACUUM will show the next blocker, and that a full list would be 20+ lines. That answer may not be enough: message #52 shows a compact summary with an extra line per co-holding class and a count of snapshot holders, so the length concern does not force a single entry. The single-line format is also what log parsers will start to depend on, so changing it in a later release costs more.
objections.author_must_show: Why should the VACUUM log name one holder when other diagnostic log lines list every holder, and would a one-line count of co-holders be enough?

critic.reasoning: A disconnected standby's slot can stay at the same xmin as a prepared transaction's xid, so the scenario is real. Message #53 defers Scott's summary to a follow-up without answering the consistency point, but later lines would be additive, so the parser argument is weak.

refuted.title: Exported blocker API is shaped for one log line and will change
refuted.failure_scenario: An extension calls GetXidHorizonBlocker() from procarray.h on a hot standby. Production builds compile out `Assert(!RecoveryInProgress())`, so KnownAssignedXids is ignored and the extension shows a wrong or empty blocker. The follow-ups planned for active/idle state, GIDs and a view then change the signature or the result struct.
refuted.argument: Message #42 limits the function to non-recovery callers with only an assertion as the guard. Messages #53 and #55 defer state, GID and multi-holder output to follow-ups. Scott's view thread in message #45 builds a separate function for the same data. A committer would likely ask that the API be static or settled before core keeps two parallel blocker scanners.
refuted.author_must_show: Why export GetXidHorizonBlocker() now rather than keep it internal to VACUUM until its shape is settled with the planned follow-ups and the view in message #45?

critic.reasoning: vacuumlazy.c calls a function defined in procarray.c, so it cannot be static, and Postgres changes such internal signatures between major versions as normal practice. The standby extension caller is hypothetical, and Scott's view is a separate uncommitted patch.

touch_points.label: WAL / replication / standby
touch_points.reason: GetXidHorizonBlocker() reads replication slot xmins and the walsender's xmin from hot standby feedback.

touch_points.label: ABI / extension API
touch_points.reason: The patch adds the exported function GetXidHorizonBlocker() to procarray.h.

touch_points.label: security / privileges
touch_points.reason: The VACUUM (VERBOSE) line can show a table owner the pid of another role's snapshot holder.

touch_points.label: maintenance burden ("who maintains this in 10 years")
touch_points.reason: A second scan must follow the horizon rules of ComputeXidHorizons() and the slot code in every later release.

touch_points.label: performance on the hot path
touch_points.reason: Each instrumented vacuum takes one extra shared ProcArrayLock scan of the ProcArray and the slots.

touch_points.label: doesn't fit what Postgres is about (extension / external tool / already solved)

questions: Which horizon inputs does v10 share with ComputeXidHorizons() and the slot code, and what fails when a future horizon source is not added to GetXidHorizonBlocker()?
When a prepared transaction and a slot hold the same cutoff, why name only one, and would one extra line with a count of co-holders be enough?
What is the full list of category strings and detail fields that v10 prints, including whether the prepared transaction GID and standby application_name remain?
How does v10 choose among several snapshot holders at the same xmin, and is the choice stable across runs?
Does a caller without pg_read_all_stats see another role's pid in the VACUUM (VERBOSE) line?

committability.owner_note: Fujii Masao is a listed reviewer and his offline comments shaped v10. The owner needs to know the ProcArray horizon computation and the replication slot xmin rules.
committability.liability: The owner signs for a second horizon scan that must match ComputeXidHorizons() in every later release, and for a log line format that log parsers will read.
committability.author_follow_up: The author has posted ten versions over a year, rebased through six CommitFests, and narrowed the scope after review.

priority.reason: DBAs who diagnose bloat after the fact gain a durable record, and several reviewers report support cases. The patch is about 31 KiB in procarray.c and vacuumlazy.c, and the duplicated horizon rules need care in later releases; nobody has reviewed v10 in the thread yet.

provisional_note: Without the code, this review could not check that the slot xmin and per-database filters in GetXidHorizonBlocker() match ComputeXidHorizons(). It also could not check the tie-break among snapshot holders or who can see the pid in VERBOSE output.
disclosure: Prepared by an AI harness; treat as a devil's advocate, not a verdict.

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert changes to CONCURRENTLY that "sped up" Xmin advance
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Revert changes to CONCURRENTLY that "sped up" Xmin advance
Reverted commit(s): VACUUM: ignore indexing operations with CONCURRENTLY
precedents_retrieved.objection:
This reverts commit d9d076222f5b "VACUUM: ignore indexing operations
with CONCURRENTLY".

These changes caused indexes created with the CONCURRENTLY option to
miss heap tuples that were HOT-updated and HOT-pruned during the index
creation.  Before these changes, HOT pruning would have been prevented
by the Xmin of the transaction creating the index, but because this
change was precisely to allow the Xmin to move forward ignoring that
backend, now other backends scanning the table can prune them.  This is
not a problem for VACUUM (which requires a lock that conflicts with a
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY operation), but HOT-prune can definitely
occur.  In other words, Xmin advancement was sped up, but at the cost of
corrupting the resulting index.

Regrettably, this means that the new feature in PG14 that RIC/CIC on
very large tables no longer force VACUUM to retain very old tuples goes
away.  We might try to implement it again in a later release, but for
now the risk of indexes missing tuples is too high and there's no easy
fix.

Backpatch to 14, where this change appeared.

Diagnosys-by: Michael Paquier <michael@paquier.xyz>
Diagnosys-by: Andres Freund <andres@anarazel.de>

precedents_retrieved.summary:

precedents_retrieved.objection:
This reverts commit aa607980aee08416211f003ab41aa750f5559712.

This test proved to be unstable on the buildfarm, timing out before the
standby could catch up on 32-bit machines where more rows were required
and failing to reliably trigger multiple index vacuum rounds on 64-bit
machines where fewer rows should be required.

Because the instability is only known to be present on versions of
Postgres with TIDStore used for dead TID storage by vacuum, this is only
being reverted on master and REL_17_STABLE.

As having this coverage may be valuable, there is a discussion on the
thread of possible ways to stabilize the test. If that happens, a fixed
test can be committed again.

precedents_retrieved.title: Switch to FullTransactionId for PGPROC->xid and XLogRecord->xl_xid
precedents_retrieved.objectors: Matthias van de Meent, Michael Paquier, Robert Haas
precedents_retrieved.summary: As a step towards 64-bit XIDs, the patches change PGPROC->xid and XLogRecord->xl_xid from TransactionId to FullTransactionId. The author presented these as changes that any 64-bit XID design would need.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Making xl_xid 64-bit adds 4 to 8 bytes to nearly every WAL record, including records that need no XID, so all writes pay a WAL overhead. Reviewers said generic structures such as XLogRecord and PGPROC should not grow, and that a patch that makes things worse now should not go in for a later gain. Robert Haas also questioned the goal of 64-bit XIDs everywhere and asked to target the specific wraparound problems instead.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
And FWIW, echoing with Matthias, making these generic structures
arbitrary larger is a non-starter.  We should try to make them
shorter.

precedents_retrieved.title: Allow single table VACUUM in transaction block
precedents_retrieved.objectors: Greg Stark, Robert Haas, Tom Lane
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch let VACUUM on a single table run inside a transaction block, so scripts run with --single-transaction would not fail; it skipped PROC_IN_VACUUM and the datfrozenxid update in that case. Later versions forced VACUUM FULL for temp tables and queued an autovacuum request for other tables, and finally added an explicit VACUUM (BACKGROUND) option.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Reviewers objected to a VACUUM command that runs in-process in some cases and as a background autovacuum request in others. Robert Haas and Tom Lane also rejected making background vacuum the default or controlling it with a GUC, because users would notice the delay and regression tests expect VACUUM to finish at once. The author agreed, switched to an explicit VACUUM (BACKGROUND) option, and proposed returning this entry and opening a new one for that design.

precedents_retrieved.title: Replica sends an incorrect epoch in its hot standby feedback to the Master
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch fixes RecordKnownAssignedTransactionIds on back branches 9.6, 10 and 11, which can move nextXid backwards on a hot standby after a checkpoint record is replayed. precedents_retrieved.objection: No one objected to the fix. The withdrawal closed duplicate commitfest entries 2462 and 2463, which David Steele marked as withdrawn at Juan José Santamaría Flecha's request, while entry 2464 for the same patch stayed open. Thomas Munro agreed that the nextXid assignment looked wrong.

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert "Add single-item cache when looking at topmost XID of a subtrans XID"
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Revert "Add single-item cache when looking at topmost XID of a subtrans XID"
Reverted commit(s): Add single-item cache when looking at topmost XID of a subtrans XID
precedents_retrieved.objection:
This reverts commit 06f5295 as per issues with this approach, both in
terms of efficiency impact and stability.  First, contrary to the
single-item cache for transaction IDs in transam.c, the cache may finish
by not be hit for a long time, and without an invalidation mechanism to
clear it, it would cause inconsistent results on wraparound for
example.  Second, the use of SubTransGetTopmostTransaction() for the
caching has a limited impact on performance.  SubTransGetParent() could
have more impact, though the benchmarking of the single-item approach
still needs to be proved, particularly under the conditions where SLRU
lookups are stressed in parallel with overflowed snapshots (aka more
than 64 subxids generated, for example).

After discussion with Andres Freund.

precedents_retrieved.title: vacuum verbose is unclear
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch changes VACUUM VERBOSE output so that each stage logs a message when it starts, rewords the heap summary line, and adds counts of pages marked all-visible or frozen and hint bits written. It also prefixes multi-line DETAIL lines sent to the client with "!" and a tab, borrowing the style of log_statement_stats.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Michael Paquier and Tom Lane objected to the server adding formatting characters to DETAIL text sent to the client. Tom Lane said the message style guidelines leave formatting to the client and forbid tabs and other formatting characters. The author did not answer that objection, the patch stopped applying, and Daniel Gustafsson returned the entry with feedback.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
The really fundamental problem with this is that you are trying to make
the server do what is properly the client's job, namely format messages
nicely.

precedents_retrieved.title: 64-bit XIDs
precedents_retrieved.authors: Aleksander Alekseev (a.alekseev), Pavel Borisov (pborisov), Konstantin Knizhnik (knizhnik), Maxim Orlov (m.orlov), Yura Sokolov (funny_falcon), Fedor Sigaev (sigaev), Alexander Korotkov (smagen), Nikita Glukhov (n.glukhov)
precedents_retrieved.summary: Change TransactionId to 64 bits in memory while keeping 32-bit xmin/xmax in heap tuples, storing a 64-bit xid_base and multi_base in each heap page's special space and computing tuple XIDs as offsets from them, with a "double xmax" fallback format for upgraded pages that lack free space. The patch was based on earlier work by Alexander Korotkov and on an implementation used in the Postgres Pro fork.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Daniel Gustafsson closed the entry as Returned with Feedback because the patch had not applied for some time and the discussion had moved to higher-level design questions without a consensus on how to proceed. Before that, Chris Travers objected that removing wraparound pressure without mitigations, such as a configurable XID-lag warning, could turn freezing and vacuum problems into later and more serious outages. The author side also stated that the thread was waiting for the SLRU-related groundwork patches to be committed first. The work was later resubmitted in a new commitfest entry.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
This patch hasn't applied in quite some time, and the thread has moved to
discussing higher lever items rather than the suggested patch, so I'm closing
this as Returned with Feedback.

precedents_retrieved.title: Replica sends an incorrect epoch in its hot standby feedback to the Master
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch fixes a bug in Postgres 9.6, 10 and 11 where a replica's nextXid can move backward during WAL replay in RecordKnownAssignedTransactionIds, so hot standby feedback carries a wrong epoch and the master ignores the replica's xmin. The one-line fix advances nextXid only when the new value is higher, as similar code elsewhere does.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The withdrawal was not a rejection of the fix. The author registered the patch in the commitfest more than once, and David Steele marked the duplicate entries 2462 and 2463 as withdrawn. The visible messages show no objection, and Thomas Munro agreed the nextXid assignment looked wrong.

precedents_retrieved.title: idle-in-transaction timeout error does not give a hint
precedents_retrieved.summary: Add an errhint to the FATAL error raised when idle_in_transaction_session_timeout ends a session, telling the user to reconnect, as the crash-shutdown and serialization-failure errors already do. A later version changed the hint text to "reconnect to the database and restart your transaction".
precedents_retrieved.objection: Peter Eisentraut argued the hint is not needed. The session ended because the application left the transaction idle, so the fix is usually more involved than a retry, unlike a serialization conflict caused by concurrent events. The author and the reviewer agreed, and the author withdrew the patch.

precedents_retrieved.summary:
vacuum verbose: show pages marked allvisible/frozen/hintbits

roaster_notes.note: The precedent list has no matching proposal, so there is no earlier rejection whose reason could apply. Inside the thread, v1 computed the blocker inside ComputeXidHorizons() and reported the wrong PID (message #12); v10 avoids that with a separate scan against the final horizon (messages #43, #51), so that reason no longer applies.
Other compatibility points look settled. The patch adds a VACUUM VERBOSE and autovacuum log line, with no new syntax, GUC, catalog or dump object, and existing lines keep their meaning.

v10 adds only a VACUUM log line and an additive procarray.h function, so it creates no on-disk, WAL, catalog or wire protocol state. Slots and walsender xmin are read, never written, and recovery is excluded by assertion. Not checkable without the code: whether the slot-xmin and per-database filters still match ComputeXidHorizons() exactly.

No security objection that would hold up. The new VACUUM (VERBOSE) line can tell a table owner that another role's pid holds a snapshot at the cutoff, which pg_stat_activity hides from roles without pg_read_all_stats. The xid owner's pid, slot names and prepared transactions are already visible to all users through pg_locks, pg_replication_slots and pg_prepared_xacts, and v10 dropped the session state, so the marginal leak is small. Without the code I could not check one point: whether the line is shown to callers who lack pg_read_all_stats.

Hot-path cost was weighed: there is one shared scan per instrumented vacuum, Laurenz accepted it in message #22, and it does not affect queries. Committers Fujii Masao and Jacob Champion are engaged, so ownership is not a concern.

Postgres has no existing feature that records, per vacuum, what held back the removable cutoff. The current views (pg_stat_activity, pg_prepared_xacts, pg_replication_slots, pg_stat_replication) show only the present state, and the existing "cutoff is far in the past" warning names no holder. No contrib module or extension I can name does this. The view-versus-log question was raised in message #26, and messages #29, #33 and #35 settled it in favour of having both.

The material shows real demand from several independent people: Fujii Masao, Sami Imseih, Dilip Kumar, Laurenz Albe, Jacob Champion and Bharath Rupireddy. Jacob and Bharath each wrote a patch for this on their own (messages #33, #40), and Scott Ray built a related view (message #45). Bharath (#47) and wenhui qiu (#54) describe concrete support cases. The cost is limited to instrumented vacuums, so demand is not a reason to reject; a remaining question is whether v10's narrower output, without active versus idle state or GID, is still useful enough.
